text: Section 245 of the Criminal Code in force at the material time (Law No. 765) provided that any law-enforcement officer who, in the course of duty and in circumstances other than those prescribed by law, ill-treats, injures or hits a person or inflicts on them bodily harm, shall be sentenced to between three months' and five years' imprisonment and temporarily barred from public service.

text: Section 86(1) of the Criminal Code now in force (Law No. 5237) provides that a person who intentionally causes physical suffering to another person, or harms that other person's physical or mental health, shall be sentenced to between one and three years' imprisonment.

text: Section 86(2)(c) of the Criminal Code now in force (Law No. 5237) provides that if the offence of intentionally causing bodily harm is committed by virtue of execution of public duties, the offender shall be prosecuted without waiting for an official complaint from the victim and sentenced to between two and five years' imprisonment.

text: Section 10 of the Meetings and Demonstration Marches Act (Law No. 2911) provides that in order for a meeting to take place, the governor's office or authorities of the district in which the demonstration is planned must be informed, during opening hours and at least seventy-two hours prior to the meeting, by a notice containing the signature of all the members of the organising board.
section_path: THE FACTS

text: Section 22 of the Meetings and Demonstration Marches Act (Law No. 2911) prohibits demonstrations and processions on public streets, in parks, places of worship and buildings in which public services are based.
section_path: THE FACTS
II. RELEVANT DOMESTIC LAW AND PRACTICE

text: Section 22 of the Meetings and Demonstration Marches Act (Law No. 2911) provides that demonstrations organised in public squares must comply with security instructions and not disrupt individuals' movement or public transport.
section_path: THE FACTS

text: Section 24 of the Meetings and Demonstration Marches Act (Law No. 2911) provides that demonstrations and processions which do not comply with the provisions of the Act will be dispersed by force on the order of the governor's office and after the demonstrators have been warned.
section_path: THE FACTS
II. RELEVANT DOMESTIC LAW AND PRACTICE

text: Section 32(1) of the Meetings and Demonstration Marches Act (Law No. 2911), as it read before it was amended in 2008 and 2010, provided that unarmed persons taking part in an unlawful meeting or procession who, instead of dispersing of their own motion after having been warned or ordered to do so and who thus have to be forcefully dispersed by government forces, are liable to be sentenced to a term of imprisonment of between one and three years.
section_path: THE FACTS
II. RELEVANT DOMESTIC LAW AND PRACTICE

text: Section 32(2) of the Meetings and Demonstration Marches Act (Law No. 2911), as it read before it was amended in 2008 and 2010, provided that unless their action breaches another criminal law provision which stipulates a more severe punishment, persons who resort to violence or making threats while being dispersed, or who resist the attempts to disperse them, are liable to be sentenced to a term of imprisonment of between three and five years.
section_path: THE FACTS

text: On 15 February 2008 the Ministry of the Interior issued a directive to law enforcement personnel on the use of tear gases (Circular No. 19).
section_path: THE FACTS
II. RELEVANT DOMESTIC LAW AND PRACTICE

text: The Ministry of the Interior's Circular No. 19 notes that, according to section 16 § 3(b) of the Law on the Duties and Powers of the Police (Law No. 2559), tear gases are listed among the weapons which law enforcement officials are permitted to use in the execution of their duties.
section_path: THE FACTS
II. RELEVANT DOMESTIC LAW AND PRACTICE

text: The Ministry of the Interior's Circular No. 19 sets out the circumstances in which tear gases may be used — both in open and confined spaces — and explains how best to obtain the maximum benefit from their use.
section_path: THE FACTS
II. RELEVANT DOMESTIC LAW AND PRACTICE

text: The Ministry of the Interior's Circular No. 19 stipulates that tear gases may not be used against persons who have stopped putting up resistance.
section_path: THE FACTS
II. RELEVANT DOMESTIC LAW AND PRACTICE

text: The Ministry of the Interior's Circular No. 19 recommends that law enforcement personnel be prepared to provide first aid to those affected by tear gas.

text: According to an information note issued by the Turkish Medical Association (Türk Tabipleri Birliği) in June 2013, CS (chlorobenzylidenemalononitrile) and CN (chloroacetophenone) gases are used by law-enforcement officials in Turkey.
section_path: THE FACTS
II. RELEVANT DOMESTIC LAW AND PRACTICE

text: According to the Turkish Medical Association's information note of June 2013, CS and CN gases damage the eyes, cause burns on the skin, severely affect the respiratory system and the lungs, restrict breathing, slow down the heart beat and cause fluctuations in blood pressure.
section_path: THE FACTS
II. RELEVANT DOMESTIC LAW AND PRACTICE

text: According to the Turkish Medical Association's information note of June 2013, prolonged contact with CS and CN gases permanently damages the cornea of the eye, upsets the heart rhythm, and has caused damage to the lungs which has led to deaths.
section_path: THE FACTS
II. RELEVANT DOMESTIC LAW AND PRACTICE

text: According to the Turkish Medical Association's information note of June 2013, the effects of CS and CN gases are more pronounced in children, pregnant women and persons with existing respiratory problems, heart problems, aneurysms, allergies and weak immune systems.
section_path: THE FACTS
II. RELEVANT DOMESTIC LAW AND PRACTICE

text: According to the Turkish Medical Association's information note of June 2013, sudden allergic oedema caused in the upper respiratory systems by CS and CN gases, as well as use of gases on persons with asthma or bronchitis, may be fatal.
section_path: THE FACTS
II. RELEVANT DOMESTIC LAW AND PRACTICE

text: According to expert reports referenced in the Turkish Medical Association's information note of June 2013, fatal doses of gases were used in operations conducted in 20 prisons in Turkey on 19 December 2000, during which 32 persons lost their lives and hundreds were injured.
section_path: THE FACTS
II. RELEVANT DOMESTIC LAW AND PRACTICE

text: According to the Turkish Medical Association's information note of June 2013, on 1 May 2007 a seventy-five-year-old man who was sprayed with gas in Turkey lost his life.
section_path: THE FACTS
II. RELEVANT DOMESTIC LAW AND PRACTICE

text: According to the Turkish Medical Association's information note of June 2013, such gases have been used extensively in two incidents in 2011 during which two persons lost their lives.
section_path: THE FACTS

text: On 3 June 2013 the Respiratory Society of Turkey (Türkiye Solunum Araştırmaları Derneği; TÜSAD) issued a press release to inform the public about the dangers of tear gas and about the steps to be taken after contact with tear gas.
section_path: THE FACTS
II. RELEVANT DOMESTIC LAW AND PRACTICE

text: According to the Respiratory Society of Turkey's press release of 3 June 2013, tear gas affects primarily the mucus membranes, in particular the eyes, throat, respiratory system and the nose.
section_path: THE FACTS
II. RELEVANT DOMESTIC LAW AND PRACTICE

text: According to the Respiratory Society of Turkey's press release of 3 June 2013, on contact tear gas immediately causes a general feeling of burning; discomfort and excessive watering of the eyes; pain and a feeling of burning of the skin and in the nose and throat; coughing; breathing difficulties; extreme restlessness and discomfort; and temporary blindness.
section_path: THE FACTS
II. RELEVANT DOMESTIC LAW AND PRACTICE

text: According to the Respiratory Society of Turkey's press release of 3 June 2013, although tear gas does not cause permanent damage in the organs with which it comes into contact, its acute effects are extremely discomforting and lead to panic.
section_path: THE FACTS
II. RELEVANT DOMESTIC LAW AND PRACTICE

text: According to the Convention on the Prohibition of the Development, Production, Stockpiling and Use of Chemical Weapons and on their Destruction of 13 January 1993 (the CWC), tear gas is not considered a chemical weapon and its use is authorised for the purpose of law enforcement, including domestic riot control, under Article II § 9(d).

text: Principle 3 of the Basic Principles on the Use of Force and Firearms by Law Enforcement Officials (Eighth United Nations Congress on the Prevention of Crime and the Treatment of Offenders, Havana, 1990) provides that the development and deployment of non-lethal incapacitating weapons should be carefully evaluated in order to minimize the risk of endangering uninvolved persons, and the use of such weapons should be carefully controlled.

text: Principle 5 of the Basic Principles on the Use of Force and Firearms by Law Enforcement Officials (Eighth United Nations Congress on the Prevention of Crime and the Treatment of Offenders, Havana, 1990) provides that whenever the lawful use of force and firearms is unavoidable, law enforcement officials shall exercise restraint in such use and act in proportion to the seriousness of the offence and the legitimate objective to be achieved.
section_path: THE FACTS

text: Principle 5 of the Basic Principles on the Use of Force and Firearms by Law Enforcement Officials (Eighth United Nations Congress on the Prevention of Crime and the Treatment of Offenders, Havana, 1990) provides that whenever the lawful use of force and firearms is unavoidable, law enforcement officials shall minimize damage and injury, and respect and preserve human life.
section_path: THE FACTS

text: Principle 5 of the Basic Principles on the Use of Force and Firearms by Law Enforcement Officials (Eighth United Nations Congress on the Prevention of Crime and the Treatment of Offenders, Havana, 1990) provides that whenever the lawful use of force and firearms is unavoidable, law enforcement officials shall ensure that assistance and medical aid are rendered to any injured or affected persons at the earliest possible moment.
section_path: THE FACTS

text: Principle 5 of the Basic Principles on the Use of Force and Firearms by Law Enforcement Officials (Eighth United Nations Congress on the Prevention of Crime and the Treatment of Offenders, Havana, 1990) provides that whenever the lawful use of force and firearms is unavoidable, law enforcement officials shall ensure that relatives or close friends of the injured or affected person are notified at the earliest possible moment.
section_path: THE FACTS

text: Principle 9 of the Basic Principles on the Use of Force and Firearms by Law Enforcement Officials (Eighth United Nations Congress on the Prevention of Crime and the Treatment of Offenders, Havana, 1990) provides that law enforcement officials shall not use firearms against persons except in self-defence or defence of others against the imminent threat of death or serious injury, to prevent the perpetration of a particularly serious crime involving grave threat to life, to arrest a person presenting such a danger and resisting their authority, or to prevent his or her escape, and only when less extreme means are insufficient to achieve these objectives, and that intentional lethal use of firearms may only be made when strictly unavoidable in order to protect life.
section_path: THE FACTS
III. RELEVANT INTERNATIONAL MATERIALS

text: Principle 12 of the Basic Principles on the Use of Force and Firearms by Law Enforcement Officials (Eighth United Nations Congress on the Prevention of Crime and the Treatment of Offenders, Havana, 1990) provides that as everyone is allowed to participate in lawful and peaceful assemblies, Governments and law enforcement agencies and officials shall recognize that force and firearms may be used only in accordance with Principles 13 and 14.
section_path: THE FACTS
III. RELEVANT INTERNATIONAL MATERIALS

text: Principle 13 of the Basic Principles on the Use of Force and Firearms by Law Enforcement Officials (Eighth United Nations Congress on the Prevention of Crime and the Treatment of Offenders, Havana, 1990) provides that in the dispersal of assemblies that are unlawful but non-violent, law enforcement officials shall avoid the use of force or, where that is not practicable, shall restrict such force to the minimum extent necessary.
section_path: THE FACTS
III. RELEVANT INTERNATIONAL MATERIALS

text: Principle 14 of the Basic Principles on the Use of Force and Firearms by Law Enforcement Officials (Eighth United Nations Congress on the Prevention of Crime and the Treatment of Offenders, Havana, 1990) provides that in the dispersal of violent assemblies, law enforcement officials may use firearms only when less dangerous means are not practicable and only to the minimum extent necessary, and shall not use firearms except under the conditions stipulated in Principle 9.

text: The European Committee for the Prevention of Torture and Inhuman or Degrading Treatment or Punishment (the CPT) has expressed its concerns over the use of pepper spray in law enforcement.
section_path: THE FACTS
III. RELEVANT INTERNATIONAL MATERIALS

text: The CPT considers that pepper spray is a potentially dangerous substance and should not be used in confined spaces (CPT/Inf (2009) 25).
section_path: THE FACTS
III. RELEVANT INTERNATIONAL MATERIALS

text: The CPT considers that even when pepper spray is used in open spaces it has serious reservations, and that if exceptionally it needs to be used, there should be clearly defined safeguards in place, including that persons exposed to pepper spray should be granted immediate access to a medical doctor and be offered an antidote (CPT/Inf (2009) 25).
section_path: THE FACTS
III. RELEVANT INTERNATIONAL MATERIALS

text: The CPT considers that pepper spray should never be deployed against a prisoner who has already been brought under control (CPT/Inf (2009) 25).
section_path: THE FACTS
III. RELEVANT INTERNATIONAL MATERIALS

text: In its reports pertaining to visits carried out in a number of Member States of the Council of Europe, the CPT has recommended that a clear directive governing the use of pepper spray be drawn up, which should include clear instructions as to when pepper spray may be used, stating explicitly that pepper spray should not be used in a confined area (CPT/Inf (2009) 8).
section_path: THE FACTS
III. RELEVANT INTERNATIONAL MATERIALS

text: In its reports pertaining to visits carried out in a number of Member States of the Council of Europe, the CPT has recommended that the directive on pepper spray include the right of prisoners exposed to pepper spray to be granted immediate access to a doctor and to be offered measures of relief (CPT/Inf (2009) 8).
section_path: THE FACTS
III. RELEVANT INTERNATIONAL MATERIALS

text: In its reports pertaining to visits carried out in a number of Member States of the Council of Europe, the CPT has recommended that the directive on pepper spray include information regarding the qualifications, training and skills of staff members authorised to use pepper spray (CPT/Inf (2009) 8).
section_path: THE FACTS
III. RELEVANT INTERNATIONAL MATERIALS

text: In its reports pertaining to visits carried out in a number of Member States of the Council of Europe, the CPT has recommended that the directive on pepper spray include an adequate reporting and inspection mechanism with respect to the use of pepper spray (CPT/Inf (2009) 8).
